source.title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Modeling
source.authors: Michihiro Yasunaga; Armen Aghajanyan; Weijia Shi; Rich James; J. Leskovec; Percy Liang; M. Lewis; Luke Zettlemoyer; Wen-Tau Yih

page_placements.theme: Retrieval augmentation and datastore scaling shift performance frontiers

record.tranche_reason: The paper examines parameter scaling in a retrieval-augmented multimodal model and reports held-out validation perplexity across model sizes, extending scaling analysis to a multimodal setting.
record.gate_note: Section C.2 and Figure 9 report perplexity scaling results for RA-CM3 and vanilla CM3. The figure does not provide extractable exact values in the supplied text, and the paper does not fit or report power-law exponents. Other reported perplexity and generation results concern retrieval design choices or model comparisons, not the scaling-law claim.
record.test_reason: Appendix C.2 / Figure 9 trains RA-CM3 and vanilla CM3 at 125M, 350M, 1.3B and 2.7B parameters and reports held-out MS-COCO image and text perplexity against parameter count. This is a parameter sweep on a multimodal (image+text) autoregressive model, so it bears on V5 in principle. However, the text gives no numbers, no power-law fit and no description of curve shape beyond the RA-CM3 vs CM3 gap. All sizes share one compute budget (two days on 256 GPUs), so larger models likely saw fewer tokens, and data may be a bottleneck. The result therefore cannot show whether a power law holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say RA-CM3 gives consistent perplexity gains over vanilla CM3 across 125M–2.7B at equal compute, with no diminishing returns in that range. They also note the 1.3B RA-CM3 beats the 2.7B vanilla CM3, and they suggest retrieval is promising at larger scale. They make no claim about power-law form.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains multimodal retrieval-augmented and vanilla CM3 models at several parameter counts and compares validation perplexity; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling results concern RA-CM3 versus vanilla CM3 and the tested parameter range; the paper reports no diminishing returns only for 125M–2.7B parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: RA-CM3 improves perplexity over vanilla CM3 at every size from 125M to 2.7B under equal compute, and the 1.3B RA-CM3 outperforms the 2.7B vanilla CM3 (§C.2, §D.1, Fig. 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of retrieval augmentation persists across model scale, so retrieval can substitute for parameters in multimodal models.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 places RA-CM3 below the FID-versus-training-compute line traced by other autoregressive models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Retrieval augmentation shifts the compute-quality frontier for text-to-image generation.

record.problems: Figure 9 supplies plotted results without extractable exact values in the provided text. The paper reports no fitted power-law form or exponents, and the tested range is 125M–2.7B parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows. Results in Table 5 vary retrieval and training design choices rather than model scale or the scaling-law form.

untested.parts: Whether multimodal perplexity follows a power law in parameters (no fit, no exponents, no readable values); video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
Not tested: no text-only pretraining loss scaling.
Not tested: no compute-optimal allocation, although all sizes share a fixed compute budget.
Not tested: FID, CIDEr and few-shot results are reported only at 2.7B, not across scale.

missing.what: Readable perplexity values per size for CM3 and RA-CM3 (image PPL axis roughly 180–240, text PPL roughly 5–20); these are needed to judge the curve shape. Could be digitised from the figure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label is dropped. The lack of a power-law fit is an untested part of V5, not a qualifying result, and all rows are cannot_determine, so no verdict can be given. The 'scaling laws' framing in the paper concerns the retrieval gain across sizes. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit or report power laws for held-out pretraining loss in language models.
No extrapolation from small runs to substantially larger runs is evaluated.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is studied.
No comparison of architecture shape at fixed parameter count is reported.

The study measures validation perplexity across model sizes in a multimodal retrieval-augmented regime, but does not fit a power law or report exponents; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream generation results are not analyzed as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitting choices or show curves bending away from a fitted power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The paper describes its size comparison as scaling laws, but its reported conclusions concern retrieval gains across scales; it neither tests nor uses the power-law claims defined here.

tranche.reason: §C.2 compares retrieval augmentation against vanilla CM3 across model sizes at fixed compute. It reports consistent perplexity improvements, but does not assess power-law form, extrapolation, optimal allocation, or another defined claim version. This is a related method comparison rather than a result testing V5.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Rows r1–r4 should link to none: exact perplexities are figure-only, and consistent retrieval gains do not establish V5's power-law form.
